C0.quote: Election of the challenger requires a majority of the votes
C0.note: Electoral-competition/lobbying model: a two-candidate majority election in which a strategic challenger makes (private) policy commitments via interest groups; coded as strategic aspects of a voting procedure. Borderline: the focus is lobbying influence rather than the voting rule itself.

C1.quote: We seek to characterize the PBEs of the no-lobbying
C1.note: Main results characterise Perfect Bayesian equilibria in which micro-targeting is (directly or indirectly) influential.

C2.1.value: votes (voters vote for the challenger or the incumbent)

C2.1.quote: votes for the challenger if and only if

C2.2.quote: vote either for or against the challenger
C2.2.note: Input is a single binary vote for one of two candidates (challenger or incumbent) under majority rule, incumbent winning ties.

C2.3.quote: Given implemented policy p, the utility of the group
C2.3.note: Voters have ideal policies on two issues, salience weights alpha and utilities W_j over policy pairs.

C2.4.note: The vote has no separate notation and the paper never says it may differ from preferences; it asserts sincere voting (eq. 2 is the sincere expected-payoff rule) without giving a reason. This matches the codebook's IDS example and C3.2 = STATED, C3.3 = NONE.

C3.1.note: Voters vote for the candidate giving higher expected payoff given Bayesian beliefs; no analysis considers voters misrepresenting preferences.

C3.3.note: No reason is given for the sincerity assumption.

C4.1.note: C2.2 is OTH (binary vote between two candidates), not RANK/WEAK/APPR/DICH/PAIR. The paper does define utilities W_j and links votes to them via the expected-payoff rule in eq. (2).

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.loc: Sect. 3.1 Influence p.35; Sect. 4-5; Sect. 6 Conclusion p.50-51
C5.1.quote: study MT in the context of social welfare
C5.1.note: Results evaluate influence (change in implemented policy) and polarisation, not welfare, efficiency, satisfaction, representation, proportionality or distortion; welfare is mentioned only as future research in the conclusion.

VOT.note: Voters vote sincerely for the candidate with higher expected payoff given Bayesian posteriors (eq. 2); not modelled as strategic (no pivotality or misreporting). STRAT was considered because the PBE definition says each agent maximises expected payoff, but the paper explicitly fixes sincere voting. info is NA by rule; the paper does state voters know the access distribution and members learn endorsements.

CAN.quote_info: The challenger only knows the distribution of the voters’
CAN.note: The challenger chooses whether to accept IG offers and which policy to publicly commit to; the incumbent is passive and implements her ideal policy if the challenger loses.

OTH.loc_behav: Sect. 3 Model, Strategies and Equilibrium, p.35
OTH.quote_behav: In that sense, IGs do not take any decision.
OTH.note: Interest groups (L, R, A, P) make offers to the challenger and endorse/inform their members; their actions are fixed (always offer their ideal policy). Coded OTH rather than BRI since they are lobbying organisations exchanging vote delivery for policy, not bribers of voters. Nature (random access) is a chance move, not coded.

C7.1.note: Challenger (CAN) is STRAT, while voters (VOT) and interest groups (OTH) are NONSTRAT in the same analysis.

C7.2.note: An argument (no lobbying cost) is given for fixing the IGs' behaviour while the challenger is strategic. No reason is given for treating voters as sincere rather than strategic, so the reason covers only part of the asymmetry. REASON chosen as the first-listed code that fits.

claims.quote: Our results may offer valuable insights into the real-world elections.
MT can be a decisive factor in close elections
This suggests why some policies are more likely to be implemented

C9.1.note: Claims about real elections, polarisation and policy implementation (gun control in the US Congress).

C9.2.loc: Sect. 3 Model, p.33-35; Sect. 6 Conclusion, p.49-50
C9.2.note: Needed assumptions: voters vote sincerely on expected payoffs (stated p.33, eq. 2); voters know the access distribution (stated p.34); challenger strategic with only distributional knowledge (stated p.33, p.35); IGs passive, only one IG gets access (stated and argued p.34-35); no office rents (argued in Sect. 6). Mapping the model onto real elections is a general model-to-reality assumption the codebook excludes.

C10.1.loc: Introduction p.27-30; Sect. 3 Model p.33-35; Sect. 6 Conclusion p.49-51

C2.4.reason: The paper states sincere voting with no reason and has no separate vote notation or text saying votes may differ from preferences, so IDS fits and DIST does not.

C7.2.reason: The paper gives an explicit argument (no lobbying cost) for making IGs non-strategic while the challenger is strategic, though not for voters.

C9.2.reason: Every model-specific assumption the conclusion's claims rely on is stated in the paper, and B's unstated assumption (that real elections fit the model) is the general model-approximates-reality kind the codebook excludes.
